title: What each join actually keeps
dek: Pick the smallest output that answers the question you actually have.
bullets: Inner — both sides must match. Drop the rest. Smallest output, cleanest intersection.
Left — keep every row on the left. Fill right-side gaps with nulls. Authoritative list + enrichment.
Right — mirror of left. Keep every row on the right; left-side gaps become nulls.
Full — keep every row from both sides. Use when neither list is authoritative.

title: Three inputs that decide whether the join is honest
dek: Each control surfaces a decision that ad-hoc scripts usually leave implicit.
bullets: Left key column — literal header name, not index. A renamed column refuses to run instead of silently dropping rows.
Right key column — same. Different names are fine; the matcher compares values, not labels.
First row contains headers — explicit checkbox. Uncheck it for headerless input; the tool uses positional keys instead.
Custom join condition — optional. Substring, composite, or non-equality joins, with the same join-mode semantics.

title: Joining two or three tables without re-deriving the semantics
dek: Use the dedicated joiner for one-off and small repeatable joins. Reach for SQL when the question gets bigger.
bullets: Two or three tables — the joiner is sized for ad-hoc merges, not warehouse-scale pipelines.
Four join modes only — no USING, no cross joins, no composite keys. Narrow on purpose.
No aggregations afterward — if you need GROUP BY, that's a SQL-shaped problem.
Inputs fit in memory — paste-and-go for CSVs in the kilobyte-to-low-megabyte range.
